text: Lessons 13 through 15 gave you four roles, each tied to a person and a domain. This lesson covers what happens when a problem doesn't fit inside one domain's boundaries: the council and committee structure above them.

Data rarely respects domain boundaries. A dispute between the customer owner and the orders owner about what counts as an active account has no single authority that covers both. That's exactly what a standing, cross-functional governance body exists for — a forum that's already there before the dispute happens, not improvised after.

Most mature programs separate this into layers. A governance council — senior leaders — sets strategy, sponsors the program, and makes the highest-level trade-offs. A governance committee is the operational layer underneath it: policy, cross-domain disputes, day-to-day decisions. And working groups handle the detailed, domain-specific work, escalating only when they're stuck.

The committee itself does four concrete things: approves the policies Chapter 4 covers, resolves disputes no single owner can settle, formally empowers owners and stewards so those assignments are visible and legitimate, and prioritizes issues when there's more to fix than there's time for.

Not every organization needs three full layers — a smaller company can compress this into one committee under an executive sponsor. What matters is that something standing and cross-functional exists. Next lesson makes every one of these roles precise, on paper, with RACI. See you there.
